output.title: Exception queues before automation
output.body:
Before you automate anything, look at the exception queue first. That is the work that falls out of the main workflow: customer questions that need a different answer, invoice mismatches, data corrections, or other cases that interrupt the day. If you cannot name the queue, you usually cannot automate it cleanly either.

The practical question is simple: which exceptions arrive often enough to deserve attention, and which ones are just random one-offs? For one week, write down three things for that queue: how many exceptions appear, how long each one takes to resolve, and what rule the team uses to decide the outcome. Then classify the queue as routine, mixed, or ad-hoc. Routine exceptions are the best candidates for a narrow automation pilot. Mixed queues still need human review built in. Ad-hoc work often stays manual, because the pattern is doing very little of the heavy lifting.

Keep the control rules visible while you do this. If the queue touches approvals, thresholds, audit trails, money movement, or other high-risk decisions, human sign-off stays in place. Automation can help organise the review, but it does not get to play accountant, judge, and jury all at once.

If the data lives in email, spreadsheets, or someone’s head, clean that up before you think about automation. A short, honest inventory of one exception queue is often the best next step.
